common_name: Dave Fleming Hardy Hibiscus (Ruby-Red Maroon-Foliage Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Named for the elder of the hybridizing Fleming brothers, this compact selection carries relaxed, overlapping ruby-red flowers ten to twelve inches across with contrasting bright-yellow anthers, set against maroon-tinted foliage. It forms an upright, well-branched clump about four feet tall and blooms continuously from midsummer to frost. Like other Fleming hybrids it tolerates drought, wind, and periodic flooding better than many older hardy hibiscus cultivars once established. It dies back completely in winter and is slow to emerge in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown.

common_name: James Fleming Hardy Hibiscus (Light Pink Purple-Foliage Compact Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: This compact Fleming introduction bears large, thick-textured, light pink flowers against purple-cast, maple-shaped foliage, staying tidier and shorter than many of the family's dinner-plate cultivars at around three feet tall. It flowers heavily and uniformly from midsummer until frost and shares the extreme cold hardiness of the Fleming breeding line, tolerating winter lows well below zone 4 thresholds. Plant in full sun with steady moisture, since hardy hibiscus growing along its native wetland margins wilts quickly if allowed to dry out. It dies back to the ground each winter and re-emerges late, so avoid disturbing the crown in early spring.
sources: University of Maryland digital plant patent collection

common_name: Copper Queen Hardy Hibiscus (Dark Copper-Foliage Pink-to-White Raspberry-Eyed Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Bred as a darker-foliaged improvement on 'Kopper King,' this Fleming selection holds refined, ovate to maple-shaped leaves in a deep bronze-purple that stays rich-colored all summer rather than fading. Huge eleven-inch flowers open light pink and fade toward white, with a raspberry-red eye whose veining streaks nearly to the petal edge. The compact, vigorous clump reaches about four feet and blooms continuously from midsummer into fall. Give it full sun and steady moisture, and expect it to die back completely each winter, emerging later than most perennials in spring.

common_name: Aquarian Hardy Hibiscus (Lavender-Pink Red-Veined Foliage Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Aquarian is a Fleming hybrid grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, with prominent red veining running through spoon-shaped, purple-cast leaves. Large lavender-pink flowers up to twelve inches across cover the four-foot shrub-like clump from midsummer into fall. It shares the Fleming line's extreme cold hardiness and tolerance of drought, wind, and occasional flooding once established. Grow in full sun with consistently moist soil, and expect it to die back to the ground each winter, breaking dormancy later than most perennial neighbors.

common_name: Royal Gems Hardy Hibiscus (Bright Pink Dark Purple-Foliage Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: First bloomed in 1985 and selected by David and James Fleming from a 'Pink Perfection' x H. coccineus seedling cross, Royal Gems forms a three-foot deciduous clump of solid dark purple, ovate leaves that undercurl slightly for a puffed, textural look. Overlapping bright pink flowers up to twelve inches wide glow against the dark foliage from midsummer into fall. It is more compact than many Fleming introductions, making it useful where a full-sized hardy hibiscus would overwhelm the bed. Grow in full sun with steady moisture; it dies back completely each winter and re-emerges late in spring.

common_name: Satellite Dwarf Hardy Hibiscus (Magenta-Mauve Purple-Foliage Compact Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: One of the true dwarfs in the Fleming breeding line, Satellite tops out at just two to three feet, well below the four-to-six-foot habit typical of most hardy hibiscus. Its magenta-and-mauve flowers are lightly veined with white, set against compact, maple-shaped leaves with a purple cast that turn golden yellow in autumn. The small stature makes it a useful choice for smaller beds and mixed borders where standard-size hardy hibiscus would be too large. Grow in full sun with consistently moist soil, and expect the plant to die back to the ground each winter.

common_name: Small Wonder Dwarf Hardy Hibiscus (White with Red-Streaked Petals Compact Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Small Wonder is a fast-growing dwarf Fleming selection reaching only two to three feet, with white flowers heavily streaked and patterned in red and pink that extend even onto the petal backs and flower buds. Foliage emerges with purple tones in spring before turning green for summer and bright gold in fall. Its compact size suits container culture and smaller gardens where a full-size hardy hibiscus would be impractical. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and expect complete winter dieback with late spring re-emergence.

common_name: Fantasia Hardy Hibiscus (Lavender-Gray Ruffled Cut-Leaf Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Fantasia stands apart from most Fleming introductions with green, finely cut foliage rather than the purple maple-shaped leaves typical of the line, paired with ruffled, rose-pink flowers with a red eye. It forms an upright, three-foot clump and blooms from midsummer into fall. As with other Fleming hardy hibiscus, it tolerates drought, wind, and periodic flooding once established, and is hardy well into zone 4. Plant in full sun with consistently moist soil; it dies back completely in winter and re-emerges late in spring.

common_name: Vintage Wine Hardy Hibiscus (Scarlet-Red Dark-Bud Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Hybridized in 2011 by Walters Gardens from a cross of 'Cranberry Crush' and 'Midnight Marvel', Vintage Wine opens near-black buds into huge, shimmering scarlet-red flowers up to seven inches across with a darker red eye, the crinkle-textured petals unfurling flat with little cupping. Flowers are produced from top to bottom of the plant rather than clustering only at the tips as in many older cultivars, on a densely upright, columnar clump of dark green, heart-shaped leaves that can add an inch of growth a day once established. It makes an especially dense, fast-filling focal point for a sunny, consistently moist border. It dies back completely each winter and emerges relatively late the following spring.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Hardy Hibiscus (Bright Pink Crimson-Eyed Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to part shade. Not to be confused with the unrelated Sweet Caroline series of ornamental Ipomoea batatas (sweet potato vine) cultivars, which share the same trade name but are a different genus entirely.

directions: Sweet Caroline bears bold, round, bright pink flowers with crimson eyes at the stem tips continuously from midsummer into early fall, opening from distinctive rose-colored buds. Large, glossy, dark green oval leaves stay attractive all season on a tall, shrubby, vigorous plant that can reach six feet in favorable conditions. It tolerates light shade better than many hardy hibiscus cultivars but flowers best in full sun with steady moisture. As with other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and is slow to break dormancy in spring, so mark its location.

common_name: Head Over Heels Adore Hibiscus (Pink Red-Eyed Wine-Foliage Compact Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; part of the Head Over Heels series bred at the University of Georgia (Ruter program).

directions: Adore rounds out the Head Over Heels series with delicate pink petals set off by a large, deep red eye, held against red-wine-colored foliage on a compact, upright plant. It tends to open its flowers slightly later in the season than its series-mates, extending bold color into early fall. Bred at the University of Georgia and distributed via Star Roses/Bailey, it shares the series' compact habit and tolerance of wet sites and some soil salinity, making it useful near low spots or in coastal-influenced gardens. Grow in full sun with consistently moist soil; it dies back completely each winter and re-emerges late in spring.

common_name: Cherub Dwarf Hardy Hibiscus (Pink Tubular Recurved-Petal Compact Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: The product of a Fleming breeding program crossing hardy Hibiscus moscheutos with tropical Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, Cherub, first bloomed in 1990, carries a distinctly tropical look despite its extreme cold hardiness: medium-sized, thick-textured, tubular pink flowers with recurved petal edges on a dense, pyramidal plant only about three feet tall. Shiny, maple-like green leaves cover the compact habit, which is notably more uniform and vigorous than many older hardy hibiscus selections. It flowers steadily from midsummer until frost and, despite its unusual parentage, tolerates winter lows well into zone 4. Grow in full sun with steady moisture, and expect it to die back completely each winter.

common_name: Little Prince Dwarf Hardy Hibiscus (Lavender Pink-Edged Compact Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Little Prince packs huge, ten-inch, luminescent lavender flowers with pink-edged, slightly ruffled petals onto a true dwarf Fleming plant only two to three feet tall. Green, maple-shaped leaves turn bright gold in fall before the plant dies back completely for winter. Its diminutive stature makes it well suited to smaller borders, containers, and front-of-bed placement where standard hardy hibiscus would dominate. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and expect it to emerge later than most perennials in spring.

common_name: Kui Nuku Dwarf Hardy Hibiscus (Medium Pink Dark Purple-Foliage Compact Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: First bloomed in 2001 by Fleming's Flower Fields breeder Gretchen Zwetzig, Kui Nuku pairs medium pink flowers with dark purple, maple-shaped foliage on a compact two-to-three-foot plant. The dark foliage turns bright gold in autumn before the plant goes fully dormant for winter. Like other dwarf Fleming selections, it suits smaller gardens and mixed borders where full-size hardy hibiscus cultivars would be out of scale. Grow in full sun with consistently moist soil, and be patient in spring since it breaks dormancy later than most border perennials.
